If it goes to court it'll have nothing at all do to with inflated balls, it'll be a simple contract dispute. Brady will claim that the NFL has no right to impose a suspension, while the NFL will read the paragraphs from the contract where it states that the league can issue suspensions based on "actions detrimental to the integrity of the game," by which they'll mean Brady's not having participated in the investigation.

The NFL will win that part hands-down. Brady refused to participate, and the NFL can absolutely suspend him for as many games as they deem reasonable. In this there will be "evidence" submitted, all of which will be bad for Brady.

The second part will be another contract dispute, where Brady will argue that Goodell cannot act as both the arbitrator and the commissioner in the case. This one's a little trickier, and a court might very well agree that Goodell needs to appoint an independent arbitrator and hold another hearing about the initial 4-game suspension (which I fully expect will still be a 4-game suspension when it's announced soon). In this the court is not necessarily arbitrating the ruling, but the manner in which the ruling was issued.

The end result will be Brady losing part 1 and winning part 2 of the court battle, but that only means that his 4-game suspension is upheld temporarily while he goes back to a 2nd round of appeal behind closed doors at the NFL HQ. In that, since the NFL will basically have won everything but the redo, the arbitrator will certainly come back with the same 4 games.

Simply put, Brady doesn't have much of a chance in court because the fight isn't about inflated balls, bad science, or cheating. The fight is about whether or not the NFL has the right to suspend a player for not participating in an investigation, and their contracts are ironclad that absolutely, yes, the NFL can do that. The only question on the table is whether or not Goodell overstepped the contract in appointing himself to oversee the appeal.
